clue.text: Man, for example, that's regularly insulted

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word insulted, starting with its first

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man, say, gets insulted on a regular basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person but is the Isle of Man; the alternate letters of 'insulted' (I, S, L, E) give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is an example of an island in the Irish Sea.

clue.text: Wonderful! A pastry's rising in layers

parts.note: super is an exclamation meaning wonderful

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the words A and pastry's are read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a tart is a pastry; with the 's it gives TARTS

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims with delight at a pastry rising in layers in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns A TARTS upwards into STRATA. 'in layers' must stand for the plural noun: strata are layers.
explanation.definitionFit: Superstrata are overlying strata, that is, layers of rock lying above others.

clue.text: One summarises it in poems, it turned out

indicators.note: turned out signals that the letters of it, poems and it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A summary writer includes a word in poems, and it turns out to matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned out' rearranges IT + POEMS + IT (nine letters); 'in' just joins the first IT to POEMS.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitomist writes an epitome, a short summary of a longer work.

clue.text: Teacher's inclination to secure hot place for retirement

parts.note: a BEd, Bachelor of Education, is a teacher's degree

indicators.note: to secure means the slope word holds the hot letter inside it

parts.note: camber is a slight slope or inclination, as on a road
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A teacher's leaning shows in grabbing a warm spot to retire to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to secure' puts H inside CAMBER to make CHAMBER. 'retirement' is going to bed, not leaving work.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedchamber is a bedroom, where one retires for the night.

clue.text: Set out plan for outside broadcast?

definitions.text: Set out plan for outside broadcast?

parts.words: Set out plan for outside broadcast?
parts.note: reads like a TV schedule for an outdoor transmission, but means scattering things about over an area, as seed is broadcast

explanation.surface: A producer lays out the schedule for an outside broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' in its old farming sense is sowing seed by scattering it widely; the answer means to scatter over, the be- prefix giving the 'outside', all-over sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestrew is to strew or scatter things over a surface, just as a sower broadcasts seed.

clue.text: Go all out to make Lorna's flat most desirable

parts.note: Lorna Doone is the heroine of R. D. Blackmore's novel, so Lorna's gives DOONE'S
level means flat
best means most desirable

explanation.surface: Someone strives hard to make Lorna's apartment as attractive as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' looks like an apartment but means level; DOONE'S is then split differently to read DO ONE'S.
explanation.definitionFit: To do one's level best is an idiom for trying as hard as possible, going all out.

clue.text: His sick tot enters hospital, having fairly high temperature

indicators.note: enters says the scrambled letters come in after the hospital letter

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

indicators.note: sick signals that the letters of His and tot are disordered

explanation.surface: A child who is ill is taken into hospital with a fever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enters' suggests going inside, but here the scrambled letters simply come after the hospital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hottish means rather hot, so a patient with a fairly high temperature is hottish.

clue.text: Restriction supported by captain of industry

parts.note: a bar is a restriction or ban
on means resting on, supported by

explanation.surface: A business leader is backed up while operating under limits.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the restriction word sits on top, resting on the word below as on a support.
explanation.definitionFit: A baron is a powerful magnate, as in a press baron or a captain of industry.

clue.text: Poem may lack this, and reason too?

definitions.text: Poem may lack this, and reason too?

parts.words: Poem may lack this, and reason too?
parts.note: free verse lacks sound-matching line endings, and the idiom 'neither ___ nor reason' means without sense

explanation.surface: A critic complains a poem lacks both structure and sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyme is what many poems lack, and the phrase 'without rhyme or reason' pairs it with reason.

clue.text: Wet blanket keeping together booty left on ship

indicators.note: keeping together says the two pieces are joined side by side

parts.note: spoils are booty, plunder
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A dampened blanket is used to hold together the loot stowed on a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet blanket' looks like a damp object but is a person who dampens fun.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoilsport is a killjoy, someone who spoils others' fun, as a wet blanket does.

clue.text: Harsh noise in time-serving vicar's parish

definitions.meaning: the loud harsh cry of a donkey
the song 'The Vicar of ...' mocks a priest who changed faith with each monarch to keep his living in that Berkshire parish

explanation.surface: A turncoat cleric's parish is filled with a grating sound.
explanation.walkthrough: A time-server shifts loyalties to suit the times; the Vicar of Bray is the proverbial example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bray is a donkey's harsh cry, and Bray is the parish of the famously time-serving vicar.

clue.text: Enthusiasm more difficult for a Cockney to voice

indicators.note: a Cockney drops the h, so the word for more difficult is spoken as a London speaker would say it

parts.note: harder means more difficult

explanation.surface: Enthusiasm is said to be tougher for a Londoner to express.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys drop initial H, so HARDER said with a non-rhotic London accent sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ardour is passionate eagerness, a synonym for enthusiasm.

clue.text: Indication of French being involved in show

indicators.note: being involved in puts the French word inside the word for show

parts.note: to evince is to show or display
de is French for of

explanation.surface: A sign that French was part of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show' is a verb here, not a performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidence is an indication or sign that something is true.

clue.text: Dejected female in famous run knocked over another woman

indicators.note: in means the female letter goes inside the run's name

parts.note: the Cresta Run is the famous toboggan run at St Moritz

indicators.note: in a down clue knocked over means the name is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: Nell is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A downcast woman is in a famous race, having knocked over another woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cresta Run is a famous ice run for toboggans in Switzerland; 'knocked over' reverses the second woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Crestfallen means sad and disappointed, a synonym for dejected.

clue.text: Part of the tuition a seamstress requires?

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A sewing lesson includes some of what a needlewoman needs.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as by example: an etui is one thing a seamstress needs.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles and pins, the sort of thing a seamstress needs.

clue.text: Rolling, turned round a yard or so

indicators.note: round means the word for turned goes around the measure

parts.note: wheeled means turned, as a column of soldiers wheels
an ell is an old measure of cloth, 45 inches, a little over a yard

explanation.surface: Something rolling spun about a yard or so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling' looks like movement but means rich, as in 'rolling in it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-heeled means wealthy; 'rolling' is slang for having plenty of money.

clue.text: Short-lived English friend crossing border with hesitation

indicators.note: crossing means the friend word stretches across, around, the border and hesitation words

parts.note: pal means friend
a hem is the border of a piece of cloth
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: An English friend's brief moment of crossing a frontier is marked by dithering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' means spanning: the friend word straddles the other two.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time, short-lived.

clue.text: Beam, adroit member of opposition being arrested

indicators.note: being arrested means the opponent is held inside the word for adroit

parts.note: clever means adroit, skilful
an anti is someone opposed, a member of the opposition

explanation.surface: A skilled opposition politician gets arrested, beaming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beam' looks like a smile but is a structural beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantilever is a projecting beam fixed at only one end, as in a cantilever bridge.

clue.text: Unusually courageous 11th-century pope?

definitions.meaning: brave as a lion, lion-like in courage
Pope Leo IX reigned 1049 to 1054; the question mark asks for his regnal number to be spelt out in words

explanation.surface: An eleventh-century pontiff showed remarkable bravery.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the pope's name, Leo IX, must be spelt out as LEO NINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonine means lion-like, and lions stand for courage; it also describes things of Pope Leo.

clue.text: Farm worker accepts pressure to renew wall-covering

indicators.note: accepts means the farm worker takes the pressure letter inside

parts.note: a reaper harvests crops on a farm
P is the abbreviation for pressure in physics

explanation.surface: A labourer on the farm puts up with pressure to redecorate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepts' puts P inside REAPER.
explanation.definitionFit: To repaper is to put new wallpaper on, renewing the wall-covering.

clue.text: Loathing displayed by hard and vengeful goddess

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and retribution

explanation.surface: Bitter hostility is shown by a harsh, avenging deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Hate is intense dislike, a synonym for loathing.

clue.text: Standard variety of low flyer

parts.note: a Roman legion's standard was topped by an eagle

indicators.note: variety of signals a rearrangement of the word low

explanation.surface: A common kind of bird that flies close to the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety of' rearranges LOW into OWL. 'Standard' looks like 'ordinary' but is a military emblem.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle owl is a large owl, a bird and therefore a flyer.

clue.text: Bar Beethoven originally omitted from greatest work?

indicators.note: omitted from says that letter is taken out of the phrase for greatest work

parts.note: best means greatest

indicators.note: originally means only the first letter of Beethoven is wanted

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Beethoven was left out of a list of the finest compositions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' gives B, which 'omitted from' removes from BEST OP. 'Bar' is a verb, as in law.
explanation.definitionFit: To estop is a legal term meaning to bar or preclude someone from asserting something.

clue.text: A theatre cat to relish

parts.note: Gus is the Theatre Cat in T. S. Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cat that lives in a theatre enjoys itself.
explanation.walkthrough: Gus, the Theatre Cat, is one of the cats in Eliot's poems (and the musical Cats).
explanation.definitionFit: Gusto is hearty enjoyment, a synonym for relish.

clue.text: Treeless plains, miles covered by father and son

indicators.note: covered by means the miles letter sits inside the word for father

parts.note: papa is a word for father
S is the abbreviation for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A father and son cross the broad grasslands, miles of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covered by' puts M inside PAPA, then S follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The pampas are the vast treeless grassy plains of South America.

clue.text: Analyse flowing water in Hampshire

definitions.meaning: a chalk-stream river in Hampshire, an English county, famous for trout fishing

explanation.surface: Someone examines a river in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowing water' is a river; the Test flows through Hampshire to Southampton Water.
explanation.definitionFit: To test a sample is to analyse it, and the Test is a river of Hampshire.

clue.text: Trendy former partner freshly presented in clumsy way

parts.note: in means fashionable, trendy
an ex is a former partner
fresh can mean cheeky, so freshly means pertly

explanation.surface: A stylish ex is newly introduced, awkwardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freshly' looks like 'newly' but means cheekily, as in 'don't get fresh'.
explanation.definitionFit: Inexpertly means without skill, so done in a clumsy way.

clue.text: View gold for Clementine's father, perhaps?

parts.note: a prospect is a view, an outlook
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Gold is seen as the outlook for Clementine's dad.
explanation.walkthrough: In the song 'Oh My Darling, Clementine', her father is a miner, forty-niner, in the Gold Rush.
explanation.definitionFit: Clementine's father in the song was a gold miner, a prospector, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Animal that's spotted golf course, say

indicators.note: say signals the word for a golf course is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: links is a seaside golf course

explanation.surface: A wild cat has been seen on the golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spotted' looks like 'seen' but describes the animal's coat.
explanation.definitionFit: The lynx is a wild cat with a spotted coat.
